```{r, results='hide'}
library(readxl)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

raw_data <- read_excel(
  "data/breaking_bad_raw.xlsx",
  sheet = "Arkusz1",
  col_names = FALSE
)

viewership <- raw_data |>
  select(
    overall_episode_raw = 1,
    episode_raw = 2,
    title = 3,
    viewers_raw = 7
  ) |>
  mutate(
    overall_episode = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(overall_episode_raw)),
    episode = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(episode_raw))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(overall_episode)) |>
  mutate(
    season = case_when(
      overall_episode <= 7 ~ 1,
      overall_episode <= 20 ~ 2,
      overall_episode <= 33 ~ 3,
      overall_episode <= 46 ~ 4,
      TRUE ~ 5
    ),
    viewers_millions = parse_number(as.character(viewers_raw)),
    change_from_previous_episode = viewers_millions - lag(viewers_millions)
  ) |>
  select(
    overall_episode,
    season,
    episode,
    title,
    viewers_millions,
    change_from_previous_episode
  )

season_summary <- viewership |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    episodes = n(),
    average_viewers = mean(viewers_millions),
    min_viewers = min(viewers_millions),
    max_viewers = max(viewers_millions),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    change_from_previous = average_viewers - lag(average_viewers)
  )

highest_episode <- viewership |>
  slice_max(viewers_millions, n = 1)

lowest_episode <- viewership |>
  slice_min(viewers_millions, n = 1)

season1_avg <- season_summary$average_viewers[season_summary$season == 1]
season3_avg <- season_summary$average_viewers[season_summary$season == 3]
season5_avg <- season_summary$average_viewers[season_summary$season == 5]

change_s3_s5 <- season5_avg - season3_avg

finale <- viewership |>
  slice_max(overall_episode, n = 1)
```

# Overview

\*Breaking Bad\* is an American television drama series created by Vince Gilligan for AMC. The series follows Walter White, a chemistry teacher from Albuquerque, New Mexico, who turns to producing methamphetamine after being diagnosed with lung cancer.\

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("BBphoto.png")

```

\
The viewership data used in this report was copied from the Wikipedia page “List of \*Breaking Bad\* episodes”. The original column is titled “U.S. viewers (millions)”.

# Viewership by episode

```{r}
ggplot(viewership, aes(x = overall_episode, y = viewers_millions)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Breaking Bad: Viewership by episode",
    subtitle = "U.S. viewers for each episode, in millions",
    x = "Episode number",
    y = "Viewers in millions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

# Season-to-season changes

```{r}
season_changes <- season_summary |>
  filter(!is.na(change_from_previous))

ggplot(season_changes, aes(x = factor(season), y = change_from_previous)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Season-to-season change in average viewership",
    subtitle = "Difference compared with the previous season",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Change in average viewers, in millions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

# Interpretation

*Breaking Bad* experienced one of the most dramatic audience increases in modern television. The first two seasons drew relatively small but steady viewership, usually around one to one and a half million viewers per episode. As critical acclaim grew, Seasons 3 and 4 showed a clear upward trend, with episodes approaching two to two and a half million viewers. The real breakthrough came with Season 5, when streaming availability allowed a much larger audience to catch up. Viewership surged to nearly six million for the mid‑season premiere and ultimately peaked at over ten million for the series finale. The numbers reflect a show that transformed from a niche cable drama into a full cultural event by its conclusion.
